newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh govt forces sugar price cut, duty to stay.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh govt forces sugar price cut, duty to stay.

text.p: Sugar traders in the Central Asian state of Kazakhstan cut their wholesale prices by up to 10 percent on Monday as part of a government-forced move to ensure low prices during the peak consumption season.

Five companies, including Man Sugar Kazakhstan, part of E D & F Man Sugar, lowered their prices to October 15, when the traditional period of higher consumption ends, according to a statement signed by the companies.

"We took this step to calm things down," said an official at one of the importers, referring to recent government remarks that importers and domestic refiners were conspiring to send prices spinning up. "After the period ends, prices will reflect the demands of the market."
The Economy Ministry said refined sugar prices had soared 52 percent so far this year to 70-75 tenge per kg, while other food products had become cheaper.

The company source said cheaper Ukrainian and Russian supplies had come onto the Kazakh market, pushing prices down and forcing six of Kazakhstan's eight refiners, which work on Cuban raws and beets, to stand idle.
The production cost for a tonne of sugar produced from beets was 38-42 tenge per kilo, he said, while the wholesale price was 32 tenge.
Kazakhstan taxes imported white sugar at 25 percent. It is keen to develop its domestic beet industry, which has contracted to a fraction of its Soviet-era level.
"We're very interested in developing beet crops in Kazakhstan, but the government should introduce severe tariffs on imported sugar," said an official from a Kazakh sugar importer.
A government statement also signed by the companies said Almaty had promised not to tax imported raws but to keep the tariff on imported whites.
The government puts annual refined sugar demand at 650,000 tonnes a year, while the companies say the real figure is lower.
Kazakhstan regularly produced 200,000 tonnes of sugar from beets in the Soviet era. Figures for output from raws were not immediately available.
Output at the two working refineries was a mere 52,150 tonnes over the first half of this year, according to Economy Ministry data.
The government said that if wholesale prices did not come down, it would unload supplies from strategic state reserves in big cities to try to force prices lower.
